Of course it is.

The beauty of Linux - and open-source software in general - is that there are hundred, if not thousands, of highly skilled people auditing the code at any given time. This isn't their job, it's their hobby, and with that comes a huge amount of passion. Very few people will be contributing the bare minimum (that you might see in a workplace), and when they do it gets reviewed/improved hundreds of times before making it into a release.

Even if there is some feature in Ubuntu you don't like, in your example activity logging/monitoring, you can uninstall it, or potentially find a fork that suits you better.

The great thing about Ubuntu is it's community. If you have an issue; ask. You'll get an answer.

The beauty of Linux - and open-source software in general - is that there are hundred, if not thousands, of highly skilled people auditing the code at any given time.

C'mon. Let's face it, that's not how it actually works. It would, in a perfect world, but that's not the world we live in.

There are some very widely used FOSS projects that receive surprisingly little attention, as far as contributions, funding and audits/reviews are concerned. Like the relatively recent mess with OpenSSL - after Heartbleed was found and widely publicized, it came to light that this library, which I'd call absolutely crucial for a large part of the Internet today, is maintained by one dude with limited funding and almost no outside contributions. Shellshock was a Bash vulnerability with a huge impact, and went undetected for 25 years... and those are just a couple of very high-profile cases. It's even worse with most smaller, less widely adopted projects.

I do think that FOSS is superior to proprietary alternatives, and I always choose it even if using proprietary software might be more comfortable in some cases - but making claims like that doesn't help anyone.

I think its disingenuous to imply that Shellshock was overlooked by auditors for over two decades. A lot of the attacks we've seen uncovered in 2014/2015 are the result of the evolution of attackers as much as inadequacies of the software. While anyone still using strcp today in C code is grossly negligent, they wouldn't be considered such in the 80's... vulnerabilities are always a function of evolution.

Attackers are starting to fuzz every layer of protocols and applications, revealing new attacks that are random and never-before-seen, that doesn't mean the software's authors are negligent (intentionally or otherwise.)

I wasn't trying to blame Bash, or the person who introduced the Shellshock bug, or anyone else. What I mean is that if FOSS was being reviewed by hundreds of highly skilled people at all times, as @NotMatt above me claims, then patterns which were fine in the 1980s, but are bad practice, now would be long gone. But they're not, because the software is not receiving that kind of attention.

I guess I'm trying to say that Shellshock wasn't overlooked by auditors - there were no auditors. (I'm fairly sure this was the case for OpenSSL; it could have been different with Bash. I really don't know.)

Another thing is that while the patterns that caused Shellshock might have been adequate in the 80s, they were obviously used in a wrong way. I mean, I have little insight into this, I'm not a developer and I don't know shit about C, but a vulnerability is a vulnerability. If I understand it correctly, Shellshock could have been used to gain root privileges in 1991 just as well as it could have been used to do that in 2014. Again, if people were reviewing FOSS code, someone would have noticed it sooner. But people mostly don't; we all assume someone else does.
I think you raise a number of good points. There is, candidly, too often an attitude of "someone else will." Thank you.

Privacy is a trade-off, and it's not binary; there's a gradient of how respectful of your privacy your OS is and it's generally in opposition to convenience. On that scale, yes, Ubuntu is more privacy friendly than Windows, but it's not as friendly as another distro like Debian, which isn't anywhere near as privacy-oriented as something like Tails.
Someone actually made a nifty website, Fix Ubuntu with screenshots so that even a beginner should be able to fix it without entering the command line.

Ubuntu is, as far as anyone knows, privacy friendly. The main searching feature (the dash) sends certain keystrokes to a Canonical server, which then obscures or strips away identifying information (like who sent it, and what they eventually chose to click on) and then routes it to different servers owned by whoever the Scope(s) points to (scopes are basically sources, when a search is done it uses a number of different scopes to find results). One of these, by default, was Amazon.

This is basically it, the extent of the damage. A few points to make about it: Canonical only gained a little money if someone actually bought something from Amazon when they found it through the dash Home lens (lenses are just separate bundles of scopes, like tabs). So not only did they not ever sell the data, but Amazon would already know what you want in the event that Canonical was being paid anything for you using the service, as you'd be visiting Amazon directly to purchase the item. And until you actually click on a search result, all these websites get are random bundles of letters being thrown at them from hundreds of thousands of people who they do not know, it's all sourced back to a Canonical server.

Not only that, but this situation is assuming you didn't turn it off in the privacy settings, or that you aren't using a different lens that doesn't connect to the network, or that you haven't simply turned off any offending scopes (which is also easy to do, if a bit tedious). The biggest problem with the Dash is that it sucks in several ways. The interface sorta sucks, and searching for things online with it is limited and kinda slow. Luckily, they have totally redesigned the Dash around the Unity 8 interface (which is currently for phones and being made for the desktop). So hopefully the service will be greatly improved in terms of UI and speed, perhaps also in the number of sources from which to search. But until then, it is perfectly useful for finding local items like apps and files. And if it is "spyware", then it truly is the least effective spyware in the history of computers.

The temptation is to use Ubuntu with proprietary and/or supplied binary BLOBs. For example, the open source Nouveau driver does not work for me, so I use NVIDIA. And perhaps I use codecs or other drivers where I am not able to inspect and compile the source myself. The Amazon spyware that is enabled by default is another concern, although it can be disabled. According to Richard Stallman, "proprietary software is software for suckers." I am inclined to agree with him, but I have practical concerns beyond his dogma. In a perfect world I'd run a pure GNU/Linux FOSS system where I could inspect and compile all the software myself. So to answer your question, it depends on how you use Ubuntu, but in practical terms I find it difficult to feel completely protected even on Ubuntu.

I'd recommend mint or manjaro over Ubuntu if you're just starting. Then as you learn more you'll be able to spend some time looking at other distros if you feel the current one isn't filling all your needs.

Back in 1981 I was auditioning for the soon-to-be-hit Broadway musical, "Cats". I was originally trying out for the role of Skimbleshanks, the orange tabby cat that lived on trains. However, after watching my try-out, the casting director told my agent that I would instead be given the role of Munkustrap, a tabby tomcat who acts as the show's narrator.

I was ecstatic at this amazing news. That night, I went out on the town with my friends to celebrate. We went to a karaoke bar and I bought all of their drinks. I returned to my cheap apartment very early the next morning, and fell asleep dreaming of the upscale condo I would buy with all the money I would receive from my new acting gig.

Two days later I received a call from my agent with bad news: I had been replaced and would no longer have any role in "Cats". Apparently a literal cat-person had shown up unannounced the previous day and sniped the role from me. I was enraged. I felt betrayed, and my bank account was wiped from all of the partying. I was kicked out of my apartment and onto the streets. I went through some very dark times, started taking hard moon sugar, and did some things I wasn't very proud of.

Eventually, thanks to na intervention from my friends and family, I was able to recover - but I have never forgiven the cat-man who took my sweet role.
